vignette:
Mateo was twenty-two years old, a product manager for a mid-sized tech firm in Austin, when he finally walked into a therapist's office six months after returning from a family visit to his hometown in northern Mexico. He had gone back for his grandmother's funeral, and during the week he was there, cartel violence erupted in the streets near his family's home. He had been caught in a crossfire while walking to the corner store-bullets cracking past him, the sudden thud of a body hitting the pavement nearby, the smell of cordite and dust. He had pressed himself flat behind a parked car for what felt like an hour, certain he would be shot, certain he would never see his parents again. He made it back inside, but something in him had not made it back at all.

In the months that followed, Mateo's body refused to settle. He felt constantly tense, as though he were bracing for another attack. His shoulders stayed hunched, his jaw tight, and he found himself scanning every room he entered-checking exits, watching hands, tracking sudden movements. At work, a colleague stepping quickly into his peripheral vision would make him flinch so hard he would drop his coffee. He started to monitor his own body obsessively: pressing his ribs to check for tenderness, inspecting his arms for any new bruise or mark, feeling his pulse throughout the day to make sure it wasn't racing. He was certain that if he could just catch the signs early enough, he could avoid being caught off guard again.

The tension became unbearable. Some nights, alone in his apartment, the pressure in his chest grew so sharp that he would dig his fingernails into his forearm until the skin broke, just to release something. He told himself it was the only way to quiet the alarm. The physical pain grounded him, briefly, but then the shame would flood in-and with it, the fear that he had hurt himself badly without realizing it, which made him check his body even more carefully the next day. This loop tightened over weeks: the hypervigilance made him desperate for relief, the self-harm gave him a few moments of quiet, and then the monitoring of his own injuries sent his threat system roaring back to life.

He also began asking his roommate, and then his coworkers, whether he seemed okay. "Do I look normal?" "Is my heart beating too fast?" "Do you think I'm safe here?" He needed someone else to tell him the danger had passed, because his own instincts no longer felt trustworthy. But the reassurance never lasted. As soon as the person walked away, his body would tense again, and he would start scanning for the next threat. The more he asked, the more he felt dependent on others to regulate a fear that never truly left.

At work, Mateo's performance slipped. He stopped taking the stairs because the echo of footsteps behind him triggered a panic response. He avoided the open-plan kitchen area where people moved unpredictably. He started arriving early and leaving late, just to minimize the number of people in the hallways. His manager noticed he had become withdrawn and hesitant in meetings, but Mateo could not explain why a sudden gesture from a colleague made him lose his train of thought. He was terrified that if he let his guard down for even a second, something terrible would happen-and he was equally terrified that the tension would tear him apart from the inside.

What finally brought him to seek help was a night he spent on his bathroom floor, knees to his chest, convinced he could hear gunfire outside his window. It was only a truck backfiring, but his body had already reacted-heart slamming, breath shallow, hands shaking. He had scratched his own forearm until it bled, and afterward he sat staring at the marks, realizing he could not keep living this way. He was afraid of what he might do to himself if the fear kept building, and he was afraid that no amount of checking or asking or bracing would ever make him feel safe again. He came to therapy because he wanted to stop the cycle, even though he had no idea how.
